source.title: Tuning the Implicit Regularizer of Masked Diffusion Language Models: Enhancing Generalization via Insights from $k$-Parity

record.tranche_reason: The study measures training and validation accuracy on a k-parity task under output supervision and masked diffusion, conceptually testing delayed algorithmic generalization but not reproducing the original modular-arithmetic setup.
record.gate_note: The parity accuracy trajectories are results bearing on the claim. The language-model test-loss and benchmark results are not rows because they do not measure delayed generalization after training accuracy saturation. Theoretical decompositions and cited results are not empirical result rows.
record.test_reason: On (20,6) parity, the study reproduces a grokking delay under output supervision. It then shows that a masked-diffusion training objective removes the delay. This is a result that V1 needs qualifying by training objective, on a different algorithmic task than the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that output supervision on k-parity groks, while the masked-diffusion objective's noise regime acts as an implicit regularizer that enables rapid, near-simultaneous generalization without grokking. Mid-range masks are fastest and boundary masks are unstable. They further claim that signal-rich mask sampling improves 50M and 8B MDLM perplexity and benchmark scores; those results do not bear on grokking.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses k-parity rather than the original modular-arithmetic setup and compares direct output supervision with masked-diffusion training. It does not test the training-set-size trend.
record.method_sensitivity: Masking interval changes the reported convergence: U[0, 0.2] and U[0, 0.3] are fastest; U[0, 0.1] and U[0, 0.4] are unstable and slower. The uniform-attention MLP also generalizes without a prolonged plateau.

fits_no_version.finding: Switching the training objective from direct output supervision to masked-diffusion reconstruction removes the grokking delay on parity. The authors attribute this to a noise-regime term penalizing output norm on unidentifiable inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The grokking delay depends on the training objective: a masking objective with an implicit output-norm regularizer yields near-simultaneous generalization on parity.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The parity experiment uses a single stated (n, k) setting, and the training-set size for the output-supervision comparison is not stated. There is no training-set-size sweep, and exact transition steps are not given in the text. Several trajectory values are presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No reported parity-accuracy result relevant to V1 was left out. Language-model losses and benchmark scores were excluded because they do not measure delayed generalization after training-accuracy saturation.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size; the training-set size N is never stated and not varied. Modular arithmetic tasks are not run.

missing.what: The training-set size N for the parity experiments and the step at which output-supervision validation accuracy rises; neither is stated in the text, so the delay length cannot be compared across studies

record.verdict_notes: V5 is related but untested. The implicit regularizer is an output-norm penalty from masking, not weight-norm efficiency, and there is no critical dataset size or ungrokking. The language-model experiments correctly have no rows. Tranche changed to T5 because the central parity result is a condition under which the V1 delay disappears. Single seed and single (n,k) setting; no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary training-set size, so it does not test whether smaller training sets require more optimization. The output-supervision training-set size is not stated.

It proposes a signal/noise decomposition and an implicit regularizer, but does not measure gradual formation of a generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, or progress measures anticipating an accuracy jump.
It evaluates language-model performance under mask-sampling changes but does not test grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data or switch delays through initialization scale or weight norm.
The large-model experiments report losses and benchmark scores, not delayed generalization during realistic pretraining or fine-tuning.
The study analyzes a masking-induced output regularizer, not a low-norm bias favoring a more efficient circuit; it does not test a critical dataset size or ungrokking below one.
It does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs or architectures.
It does not test whether grokking is caused by adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits in the softmax.
